utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation you made to tell the truth here. Now, that still applies today as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has some more questions to put to you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Malaj. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I'm counsel for Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, the accused in this case, and as Mr. President just indicated, I would like to ask you some questions to clarify some facts that you spoke about yesterday while you were examined by my learned friend Mr. Matthias Neuner. My first question is: Can you tell us where your village is in relation to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our village is in the outskirts of the city of Gjakove. It's 5 kilometres from Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Djakovica is in Kosovo and Metohija. I asked you how far your village was from the Albanian border. Your village is Korenica. That's your village, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but the border is far away. You can go to the border through Qafa e Prushit, but we are not close to that area. I don't know how close or far to the border crossing we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: Is your village in the border zone, and do you know what the term "border zone" means?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what the border term means, but we're not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask the usher to show a map bearing the number P002-295. I would like it to be shown to the witness, P002-295. Could we please zoom in on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, you marked your village with number 1, if I'm not mistaken, and the markings in red ink, those markings are already admitted into evidence. We can see the town of Djakovica, but I can also see the border, the border between Albania and Serbia or, rather, Kosovo and Metohija. So could you show us where the border is by taking the same pen and mark the borderline with Xs, with a number of Xs, so that we can confirm that we both see the border in the same place, if of course you see it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, how is it going to help this Chamber to have a witness such as this lady attempt to draw a borderline when there is, on authoritative maps, a very clear and correct border? Do you see my concern? I don't see how we are going to be helped in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully understand your concern and this that issue you've just raised, Your Honour. The reason why I'm asking this is because this will elicit a series of questions on my part. Let me tell you, we're talking about 1999 and 1998 and the statement that this witness made, that the villagers from the village had gone into the mountains, so where the mountains are. so I just want to see whether this witness herself is able to indicate the border which is shown here, and this is not controversial at all. And I understand why you're asking me this, because we all know that this is a proper map. I just want to see whether the witness herself knows that, knows where the border is. Nothing else. So if you'll allow me, if she could merely indicate where she sees the border, and if she cannot or if she is not to do that, I will comply and I will go on with my questions. But you can see that it is rather illogical. We can all see how close the border is. But I just want to check whether she is able to tell where the border is, because she was able to show various locations on the map, to the east, to the south-east, to the west, to the north. So if you allow me, I would like her to show us the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see on the map displayed on my screen the part of the map that shows the border, but are you saying that the border is depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I can see the villages that are in the territory of the Republic of Albania on this map, but if anyone should know that, it's the witness. She lived there. But if not, then perhaps we can use some other map. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't have any Albania on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I will withdraw this question, and I will not insist on this map being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's the name of the mountains next to your village?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mountains close to our village, they are next to our village as a matter of fact. When you leave the house, you have the mountains there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What are the mountains called?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mountains of Korenice. There is no other name in the place where we live. That's where our land is, where our mountains are, where our village is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do those mountains surround the whole village, or where are they? Are they to the north, to the east, to the south, or to the west, or is it that they are all around the village?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere there is -- you can see the mountain. The rest of it is a low area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are those mountains to the north, to the east, to the south, or to the west? Can you give us the point of compass?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that beyond those mountains there is the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are a lot of villages you have to go through before you reach where you are saying. We are not on the border zone, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next line of questioning will have to do with the Micunovic family. Yesterday you said that Dragan Micunovic was the only Serb in your village, and in your statement of the 6th of September, 2001, at page 2, para 2, you say that in your village there was the Micunovic family and there were 15 family members. Now I want to ask you whether you still maintain that the only Serb in the village was Dragan Micunovic, or was that a linguistic error, or was this a family with 15 members?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the only one in our village, but I mean the whole family. He had three brothers, and their family lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned his three brothers, and you said that they lived there too. Am I understanding you correctly? Or was he the only one?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the only household.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How many members were there in the household, approximately? You don't have to give us the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were 15 of them, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as regards Dragan Micunovic, you told us yesterday that he was an officer in the Yugoslav Army, yet in your statement when you mention him for the first time, you say that Dragan Micunovic was, in fact, a major in the Yugoslav Army. The term that you used yesterday is the broader term. What you said in your initial term; is that correct? Was he a major in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main thing is that he worked there. Whether he was an officer or a major, that is where he worked, in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you, on the 6th of September when you gave your statement, that was in 2001, say that Dragan Micunovic was a major in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, but he used to play all the roles possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Micunovic, who is that?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: His brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was he also an officer in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what rank he had?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was an officer or not, I don't know, or what rank he had. But I know that he worked in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, as regards Aca Micunovic, whom you mentioned yesterday, you said he was the local village policeman. In your statement of the 31st of August and the 1st of September 2001, you said that Micunovic was a police officer and that he worked in Korenica in that capacity. Can we agree that he was just an ordinary police officer, that he did not have any special rank?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we used the term "local policeman," and with that term we meant a policeman in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's much clearer. You said that you were on good terms with the Micunovic family until the 4th of April, 1999. This is what you say in your statement of the 6th of September, 2001, at page 2. But you also say something before the sentence. You say that the three brothers behaved as if there were 300 Serbs living there. How are we to understand this sentence?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up until that day they behaved very well. We went to social occasions together, weddings and so on. But they behaved very badly when they forced us out, returned us back, and then they did whatever they wanted with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that for all three brothers that I mentioned - Aca Predrag and the eldest brother, the officer Dragan - or just some of them?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Predrag do anything, at least not to my family. Aca Micunovic, after he forced us out of our homes, he told us to go back again. Dragan and Aca gave orders to separate the women from the men, to tell the men that they had to go to the mountains, and then he gave orders to the men to go back to their homes again. Whatever orders he gave, we obeyed them. Whatever he said, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's much clearer now. Mrs. Malaj, my next question, in fact a whole series of questions, will pertain to the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army. Can you tell me what does this name mean to you? When you say Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA, what do you understand it to mean, you personally?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosovo Liberation Army, to me it has a good meaning. At that time, however, we were not members, and we did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of an organisation is it?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was a housewife with five children. At that time I was trying to get food on the table and feed my children. I was not involved in any such organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is whether you knew what kind of an organisation it was, not whether you took part in it. And I fully understand the role that you played, the role of a mother.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Malaj, please tell us, how far from Korenica are the villages of Nec, Smolnica, Pacaj, and Ramoc?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nec and Ramoc are next door to us. Smolice is far away; it's not close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about Pacaj?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the other side. It's not close, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far away from your village are the villages of Pacaj and Smolnica, in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. I've never been to Smolice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that in 1998, together with the other villages, you would leave Korenica because you were afraid because the Serb forces started opening fire at the villages of Nec, Ramoc, and other villages, that were, as you said, close to your village. In your statement of the 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2000, at page 2, paragraph 5 - page 2, that's in B/C/S; it's in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when quoting the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said: "We were afraid because the Serb forces started firing at the KLA positions in the villages of Nec, Smolnica, and other villages, in the Caragoj valley. You do not mention the KLA positions in your evidence yesterday. Now you tell us that you don't know what this is all about, so why did you say that yesterday, whereas on an earlier occasion you said something else? Could you please explain this obvious discrepancy between what you said in September 2000 and what you said yesterday in your evidence. This is the statement that you gave and that you signed as your statement, unless now you want to tell us something else.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, could you speak more slowly and explain things better. I don't know which question to answer first. When the forces were there, I told you that they were in May, they shelled from the positions -- or shots were fired from the position of Ramoc and Nec, but I don't know, to be truthful, I don't know because we were not involved in anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The shots were fired into Ramoc and Nec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... getting an explanation, and let me repeat, I will be slower. I don't know how fast the interpretation was. So your statement on the 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2000, in Albanian the reference, and the Croatian, Serbian, Bosnian, and in the English versions, I provided the exact reference as to where those words are in your statement. This is not something that you should be concerned with, but you should be concerned with the essence. I wanted to explain the discrepancy between what we heard from you today, yesterday, and what we were able to read in your statement, if it is indeed your statement, and I believe it is. Yesterday it was not controversial. The statement of the 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2000. You said: "We were frightened because the Serb forces started firing on the KLA positions in the villages of Nec, Smolnica, and other villages in the Caragoj valley." And now you tell us you don't know about Smolnica, yet you were saying something about it at that time. You said that you didn't know what the KLA was, that for you it was something positive. I understand that you're now saying that you don't know what kind of an organisation it is, but in your statement you say they started opening fire on the KLA positions. How come that now and yesterday you didn't tell us anything about that? You don't even mention that. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that they fired at those positions; however, where they were positioned, that I don't know, whether it was Nec, Ramoc, or Smolice, we didn't hear them. The forces were moving along the main road Gjakove-Runik. We were at Korenice. They would stop; they would fire at those positions. But as for the exact locations, where they were positioned, that I don't know. To tell you the truth, I really wanted to see the KLA, at least one member, but at that time we were very busy and we didn't dare even go further than our courtyard, to schools or to the church. We left our village. We went to Guska. It was impossible to go beyond our village because of the forces at that time. This was the situation. It is true that I've mentioned it in my statement, that they were there in Nec and Smolice, but exactly where, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And how come you didn't mention it earlier today or yesterday, instead of mentioning the KLA, you say you don't know what the KLA was all about, that you don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will not insist on that. I would like to move on and say -- can I conclude that you never met or were introduced to a single member of the KLA in 1997 and in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1997, not in 1998, not even in 1999. After the war ended and when NATO entered Kosova, after we returned from Albania, it is only then that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Fila Malaj? If you do know that person, can you tell us who that person is and where do you know him from?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Fila Malaj. She is our first cousin. Our fathers are brothers. We are both married to the same family, in the Malaj family. We live close to each other; our houses are next to each other -- close to each other. We live in the same village. Her husband and her son were killed, and her house was burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How far is her house in Korenica from your house?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Fila's house from my house? It's not that far. There's only one wall between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you socialise, the two of you?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What do you mean? In what way, socialising?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You were cousins. Your fathers are brothers, as far as I can understand. So I'm thinking that as first cousins and neighbours, you must have socialised. Did you go to church together? Did you drink coffee together? Did you visit each other?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That, yes. I thought your question referred to the period when we left our houses, but what you said is true, we did socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of October, 2001, your cousin stated to the OTP that she personally knew that the KLA manned the front lines in Ramoc, Nec, Junik, Lug, Caragoj all the way up to the Kreca river, and that was in the immediate vicinity of your village. Since you are so closely related and since you socialised, which is understandable, I really don't understand how come you don't know anything about the KLA as it was at that time and she knows so much and you're so close.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we didn't talk about the KLA or things like that. I don't know anything about Ramoc and Nec and that part of the area. I also told you that there were there, the KLA, but personally I didn't see them. We did talk about things, family things, about our children, about a better future for our children, but we didn't talk about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, are you familiar with Shpend Malaj? Does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have a Shpend Malaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is he a person from your village?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a Shpend Dushmani, but not Malaj, in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Milutinovic case, page 1362, line 8, to a similar question put to you by a different counsel, you answered yes. You said that you knew who Shpend Malaj was. How come you don't know who that person is today?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no Shpend Malaj in my family. Please, we don't have anyone by the name of Shpend in my family. In the village there is a person by the name of Shpend, but not by the surname Malaj. There is a Shpend Dushmani. I do know this person. We were at school, part of the same generation, but we don't have a Shpend Malaj in the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who's Shpend Dushmani?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also had his father, his uncle, his first cousin, and two brothers killed. He lives in Korenice, in my village. I don't know what else to tell you about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Gani Malaj? Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't have a Gani Malaj in the family either. We don't have male members by this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make things clear, are all the Malajs in Korenica members of one family, or, rather, when you say "we don't have a person by that name in our family," do you only refer to your inner family?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are four Malaj households in Korenice, but you will not find a Shpend or Gani Malaj as members of these households. So we are four households, we are related to each other, but we don't have any Gani or Shpend as members of our family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what about Islam Malaj? Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, they do not belong to my family. If you want, I can mention all the names of the members of the Malaj family. You will find many people with the last name Malaj, but these that you mention are not part of my family, nor is Shpend or Gani or Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you about two more names. Adrian and Valdet Malaj are the names.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adrian Malaj at that time was very young. He lived in Switzerland. He did not live in Korenice at the time, but he is part of our family. And the other name that you mentioned, that I don't know. Did you say Lundrit or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Valdet.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't have a Valdet in our family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You've said about Shpend, Gani, Ismet, and Valdet that you don't know who they are, and you only mentioned Adrian as a person you knew. He resided in Switzerland when the conflict started. You said that Adrian was very young at the time. Do you know that he was a member of the 131st Brigade of the KLA? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please, it cannot be him. He was very young. He left for Switzerland at the age of seven, and he was not there at the time in Kosova. And as I said, he was very young. This must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've asked you all this because I have information about some people. And let me ask you if there was anybody from Korenica or its surroundings who went by the name of Adrian and by the family name Malaj and did not belong to your family. Would that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You won't find another one in Korenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that in the course of 1998 you would go to the mountains with the men but that the men would do it more often on their own. Would the same thing be happening in early March 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men would go to the mountains for shelter because in the morning they would undertake actions; they would go to houses. So that's why the men went to the mountains and then would come back in the evenings to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that this is contrary to your statement and your testimony provided yesterday. You said that there were no problems with either the military or the police before April 1999, that they were a mere presence there, that they did not ill-treat anybody. They were there just to supervise, as it were, and I'm quoting you. Why would men retire to the mountains? I can't understand. If your statement is correct, as I quoted it just now and as you stated yourself, can you then answer, how come that the men went to the mountains?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men went to the mountains because they were scared. We were all scared. The infantry forces, for example, in the spring, they were just above my house. So the men would go to the mountains only to protect themselves, for shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the -- there was no freedom of movement or, rather, that it was limited. How did they go to the mountains, and having asked you this, I accept that your statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretly, by hiding themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At night?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, around 4.00 in the morning, when they would not be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the women?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women would remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I then conclude that the men went to the mountains because they were afraid and that the women stayed behind because -- I really don't see why.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason is because they were going after the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that nobody had been persecuted before April 1999, that they were a mere presence and that they just supervised the situation.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't persecute because people would not leave their courtyards. They would leave secretly, early in the morning when they could not be seen. However, had they seen anyone moving about, they would probably shoot them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Gjon Prelaj, a 15-year-old boy who allegedly conveyed Dragan Micunovic's orders to the village of Korenica to take to the mountains. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is a person who brought their order to us. They issued the order to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Their order or Dragan Micunovic's order? Whose order?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Micunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "to us," "they ordered us," who was it who the 15-year-old boy conveyed Dragan Micunovic's order to?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To everyone in the village. So every man in the village left for the mountains. There were rumours that trucks and other vehicles would come to take us to other locations. So amongst the group that left for the mountains was my son, Blerim Malaj. My husband took him with him. He didn't know why he was going there. So when he went to the mountains, he asked his father why we are here, and my father said -- and his father said, for them not to be seen. So they went to the mountain on that day and then they came back in the evening, at his orders again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is your statement in which you say to the investigator of the Tribunal as follows: "The order said that all the men had to go to the mountains to hide. This is what the order said." Are these your words?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was that an order? Was that, rather, a warning? A military can also order somebody to stay put, not to move, and here you say that the order was for everybody to go to the mountain to hide. My question is this: Was it maybe a warning issued by your neighbour Dragan Micunovic to everybody to hide?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, I beg to differ. If somebody says to somebody else to hide, to save themselves, how can that be an order? But let's leave it at that. Let me move on to something else. When did the men return from the mountains? Or maybe you wanted to say something else, and I'm sorry if I interrupted you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men returned on the same day. I wanted to say the following: They separated the men from us for them to go to the mountains and for us, the women and children, to be taken to new locations. This was the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're confused about the time, place, and people involved in the events. You said in your statement, and you agreed with that but I'd like to go over that again, you said that Dragan Micunovic, your neighbour, said to a child whose name is Gjon Prelaj, that he ordered all the men to the mountains to hide, and now you are saying that they separated the men from everybody else. Who did that, Gjon Prelaj? I can agree that this did happen at one point, but maybe not on that day. I know that you did say that the men were separated from the women when the convoy was being organised and when you suffered a terrible tragedy. I know all of that, Mrs. Malaj; I'm not denying any of that. However, what you just told us now, I apologise, would you please be so kind and to make an effort to explain things for everybody so as everybody in the courtroom may be clear on what really happened.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The day Dragan Micunovic issued his order to the young man, the 15-year-old Gjon, Gjon Prelaj, this day was terrible. The word was that the men would go to the mountains and the women would be taken to other places. This is what I stated in my statement. But they made the men come back on the same day. This was in the evening. I don't know the exact time. We were terrified; we were worried. He, my son, when he came back, he said to me that he was very scared, that he would never leave me. Nobody knew what was going to happen to them in the mountains, but luckily they came back. But, as I said, until the 27th, they didn't do anything anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The men left and hid in the mountains on that day. And what about the women? What happened to them? Did anybody touch them, ill-treat them, harass them, or humiliate them in any way?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing happened to us. We were expecting something to happen because the word was that we would be taken to other locations. But nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when it comes to the men going to the mountains, I showed you a part of your statement where you stated that you, yourself, also went to the mountains; is that correct? Did you go to the mountains as well? On what occasions? How many times? What were the reasons behind your decisions? And if I misquoted you, please say so.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count how many times we went to the mountains. The reason was because they would stop on the road - our village is by the road - and they were shooting from there. So we left the village and went to the mountains to protect our lives and not to suffer any harm. But we were tired of leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you some questions about the statement you provided yesterday. You said that in the spring of 1998 you'd seen tanks. You also said in your 31st of August statement that there had been five of them. However, you said that it was in 1999, before the 27th of April, when tragedy struck your household. Because of what you said yesterday and because of what you stated in 2000, and that was that you had seen five camouflage tanks, rather large ones, in 1998, and also in your statements provided on the 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2000, you also mentioned five tanks but you said that they appeared in 1999. Can you please now explain whether you misspoke, whether your words were incorrectly recorded, if there was a mistake? Can you clarify, and then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a mistake. The first time we saw them was in 1998, and there were tanks all the time, even later on. But the first time we saw them was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now, this is the first time you're saying it. You never said it before, either in your testimony so far or in your statements. If things are as they seem to be, let's go to the year 1998. You said yesterday that you'd seen tanks. How many tanks did you see at the time in 1998? Were there five? You keep on mentioning this number, five, and again you say five in 1999 and that's why you have confused me.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in 1999. There were countless tanks in 1999, while in 1998, when I saw them for the first time, there were five tanks. They were on the road from Gjakove to Junik and the infantry, they were all above my house passing there. And then from 1998 to 1999 until the war was over, there were countless tanks, innumerable tanks. The first ones I saw were five tanks on tracks, and everything is clear in the statement. However, from that day to the end of the war, the tanks we saw were innumerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, those five tanks, we heard that they were tracked. What colour were they?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue camouflage, green camouflage. So blue camouflage, those colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that you saw a blue tank with tracks?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What did you see on those tanks? What kind of equipment did they have mounted? Was anyone walking in front of them or around them or behind them or moving in any other way?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please, they were on the main road from Gjakove to Junik. I couldn't see what they had on. We have a two-storey house, and we could see them from our house. Well, of course they had their own guns, the usual guns. Why were they tanks -- those tanks there? There's this mounted gun on the tank that you can turn around. I don't know the name of the gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's all fine and well, Mrs. Malaj, but let me remind you again of your statement you gave in September 2001 when you told an investigator of the OTP something completely different. You said: "On the same day on the main road I saw five large camouflage tanks and two police officers on each." How come those two police officers have gone missing now from your evidence today? You said quite specifically that there were no persons on the tanks. That's what you said today. And on the 6th of September, 2001 -- well, it's not funny. You say: "We saw two police officers on each tank." Now I'm asking you, how come that the police officers have now gone missing?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which officers are you talking about? Of course somebody was driving the tanks. And I mentioned before that there is a gun that's mounted on the tank and it came around, and how can it come around with somebody moving it around? Of course the policemen were there. I don't know whether they were officers or not. They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malaj. This is quite sufficient. I have to go back to those blue tanks. What did those tanks look like, those blue tanks? Please describe them. Were they the same as what you described to us a little while ago, only blue?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, blue camouflage. There were some one-coloured machines as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Blue camouflage? What's this blue camouflage colour? Can you describe that to us?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you say darker blue and lighter blue, mixed. We call it "teget."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, you mentioned a Pinzgauer vehicle. Could you please tell us, what is it? What kind of a vehicle is it?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's got a tarpaulin on top; it's covered - that's how I know them - or "kampanjolas."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move on to the events of the 4th of April, 1999. At what time did Milutin Prascevic come to your village on the 4th of April, he himself?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, but I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it closer to noon or closer to the evening, Mrs. Malaj?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, how many police officers came with him? You said that they came in cars, in vehicles, but how many vehicles and how many men?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milutin Prascevic came in one car. He stopped close to Engjull Berisha's house, close to the transformer. He went to the Dedaj family and gave the order for the whole village to leave. Then he came to my house together with another policeman, both of them armed, and he ordered us to leave the house, leave the cars behind and take the tractor. The whole village did whatever he said, whatever his orders said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us this yesterday. That's what you told us yesterday, and that's why I interrupted you, lest we should waste time. And I can see now that the time for our break is drawing to a close. I would like to complete this line of questioning before the break. Mrs. Malaj, so let me ask you things that are not clear to the Defence and that are important for the Defence, because we believe that it is crucial for the trial, things that you did not say or things that are, in the Defence's view, contrary to the facts. But I don't want to argue anymore. Mrs. Malaj, do you understand Serbian? Do you speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How much? Well, your children went to school and they were marked 1 to 5, so how would you mark your Serbian? How much do you understand it? It would be -- would it be 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5? I'm sure it's not 5. But how well do you speak Serbian? Be frank.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to school I received the marks 3 or 4 in Serbian, but from that time on I haven't practiced it much. I just know enough to get by.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now it's much clearer. So you did understand Serbian. The reason why I ask this question has to do with Mr. Prascevic because he addressed you. You asked him something. In what language did you ask him? What did you ask him? You asked him what his name was. In what language did you ask him that? What did you say, "Ko si ti," who are you?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke Albanian to him. I asked him, Who are you, and he said, I am Milutin Prascevic. And he said, Madam, you can leave your home. Take the whole family with you. Leave the cars behind. I spoke to him in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that Mr. Prascevic understood very well what you asked him, since he gave you this answer?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he spoke very good Albanian. He spoke very good Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. Thank you. The order to leave your homes, was it given in Albanian by him? Was it an order? How did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Albanian, both at our home -- when we were at our home, but also to the whole village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time for our break. I have maybe 10 or 15 minutes to complete this line of questioning, but I don't want to use up all the time. I know that there are some technical issues here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break now and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Milutin Prascevic spoke to you in the English -- rather, in the Albanian language. Who was present there at the time when you asked him who he was and when he told you what he told you? So who was there with you, next to you?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family, the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you standing next to your husband, in fact, when you asked him this?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did your husband speak to him at all, in addition to what you told him?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both of us spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what did your husband talk about with Prascevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, just we were ordered to leave the house, and we did. He said, You have to get out. My husband said, Okay, and I said the same, and that's happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: Had you seen Milutin Prascevic at all before that occasion? Did he look familiar to you? And if you knew him, where did you know him from?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him from before. I knew him only on that occasion, got to know him on that occasion, because he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know today where he was from, where he lived, where he served?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time he lived in Gjakove, he served in Gjakove, but I don't know where he was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: You were told to leave that evening, your family and the whole village. Where were you told to go?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told in my courtyard, in my house. That's where he came to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did not understand my question. You were told to go where, to leave your houses and to go where?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 6th of September, 2001, in the third sentence at page 1 you say: So two years after the event, this is what you're saying, first you say, "They ordered us to go to Meja" and then two years later you say they ordered us to go to Albania, and today you again say to Albania. Yesterday you said to Albania. What was the reason? Why did you say first that you were to go to Meja, and you reached Meja, and you will agree with me that it is very close to your village, 2 to 3 kilometres away from the village in the direction of Djakovica, and now you say that you were told to go to Albania. Could you just very briefly tell us what this is all about? Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered to go to Albania, but before you go to Meja, because the road Korenice-Gjakove goes through Orize, Suhadoll, Meja, Brakoc, and then Gjakove, the town. That day we were not able to go to Orize. We were told to go back. We were told to go back home by Aca Micunovic together with another policeman. They came by car, and they told us to go back home, and because he told us so, we turned back and went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the reason for all that, why you were told to go back home? Because you will agree with me that place is 2 or 3 kilometres away from your village, that location that you reached and you were then told to go back.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place we reached is only 1 kilometre from Korenice. That's the name of the village Suhadoll. Of course they were playing games with us. That's why they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the local police personnel, you say that Prascevic was an employee in Djakovica, which is 5 kilometres away from you village. Now you mentioned Aca. I suppose that it would be Aca Micunovic. Was there anyone else there, other policemen that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my learned colleague. I'm just rising because I needed some time to check the reference given by my colleague in his earlier question, and I just wanted to bring this on the record. As far as I understood the question, it related to the fact whether the witness had said in her earlier statement that Mr. Prascevic said that she was to go to Meja, and I've just checked the statement and I don't find -- the statement of 6 September 2001, and I don't find any reference to Meja in it. I just wanted to bring this on the record. According to the statement, it says that police officers came to the village. The order was to go straight to Albania. So insofar -- I believe the witness was consistent. I just wanted to put this on the record as wrongly quoted. I don't find any reference to -- that the witness had stated that she was told to go to Meja. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have the exhibit reference to the statement, please, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As far as I know, the statement was not tendered by my learned colleague this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I certainly haven't tendered it either because I had full examination-in-chief, Your Honours. It's not in evidence, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You heard what Mr. Neuner has to say, Mr. Djordjevic. Is there some other reference that you were referring to in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully take into account this intervention by my colleague, Mr. Neuner, but not -- in order not to waste time, I will now continue examining the witness and I will go back to this issue later to provide an answer to the -- my colleague. I will ask my case manager to check -- to see whether I had, indeed, made a mistake. But with your leave I will now continue questioning the witness. I will change the line of questioning, and I will answer -- provide an answer later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would certainly look forward to hearing your answer, Mr. Djordjevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will now continue cross-examining the witness, and I will go back to this issue once I have checked everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, do you know, are you aware of the fact that Mr. Prascevic, the man that we have been talking about, was killed in Meja on the 21st of April, 1999, in the afternoon, and that two Serb policemen were also killed - Boban Lazarevic and Lugdrag Lazarevic. And an Albanian Naser Arifaj was also killed and another Serb Miladin Docic [phoen]. Do you have any knowledge of that incident?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were killed but no more than that. I heard, as everybody hears of something, but I don't know anything else about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't know anything about that, I will not be asking you any other questions about the circumstances of this incident. To complete this set of questions, I have several things to ask you about, things that have to do with 1999 when you were telling us about the tanks. In your statement you spoke about five tanks in 1999; today you corrected yourself, saying there was a mass of tanks, that you didn't know how many there were. Now I have to ask you: Why didn't you say so before? Why did you wait until today to say it?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point was when we saw them for the first time, when we talked about it. After that date we saw them almost every day. It was something that happened every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the time when NATO air-strikes were already well underway, April 1999. Could you tell me, did you hear the aeroplanes flying over Djakovica and in the area around you, NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And since you were able to see so many tanks, did you see the NATO aircraft bomb those tanks? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the NATO aircraft bombing them. We could hear the noise but we didn't see them, the actual bombing, at least I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So we will agree that you did not see NATO aircraft destroy a single tank or some kind of an armoured fighting vehicle, and you told us that there were so many of them.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my village, when we saw the tanks every morning going on, moving on the Gjakove-Junik road, on that morning they didn't bomb. In the mornings the Serb forces usually undertook offensives on the villages, as was the case with our village on the 27th of April. During our stay in Korenice, NATO did not bomb anything. Nothing happened from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, now we come to the 27th of April, 1999, and this terrible event, terrible for you and your family, when you lost your son and husband, your next of kin, and I'm really sorry for it, but I have to ask you this: Can you tell me who were the soldiers who entered your yard that morning? What were they dressed like? What were they shouting? How did they speak? And how did they get there? You told us what weapons they had so I'm not asking you that.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My yard was encircled by them, by 35 of them, with tanks, Pinzgauers. They approached my house by firing gun-shots, speaking in Serbian. My yard was full of them. Around the house there were 35 of them. My house was tightly surrounded by them. My son Blerim Malaj, who at the time was 15 and a half years old, on that morning happened to be in the toilet outside the house. He was the first one to be stopped by them. The second -- secondly, policemen, soldiers dressed in blue camouflage uniforms, they were all there. It was a terrifying experience. When I saw my son lying on the ground, a policeman or a soldier - you are here to verify that because we thought that only the army had long-barrel weapons, not the police - I started to scream when I saw my son lying on the ground. The police or the soldier forced my son to turn his head on the other side so that he could not see me. We had three cars in the yard. One belonged to us, to my husband, and two, to my brothers --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will have to ask you -- well, we heard this evidence from you already. We heard about this terrible event yesterday. That's why I interrupted you. It is very difficult for me to ask you about the events of this date, but I have to do it as a professional. Now, regarding the army that entered, the troops that entered your yard, you told us there were 35 of them. It's a very exact figure. Did you count them? Is this how you know that there were 35 of them? This is very important for us. We need you to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 35, maybe more. It couldn't have been less than that. But I did say 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just asking you this because that's a large number of people, and it would take you a long time to count them and you need to be very perceptive. Now, my next question is: Were they all dressed in the same way; and if so, could you please describe it in as much detail as you can, as far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, some wore masks; some had red ribbons around their arms; some were dressed in blue uniforms. They were in my yard, inside my yard, four or five of them, with red ribbons, with painted faces, and they were holding their automatic rifles on the heads of my son, my husband, my brother, three of them. And they, my husband, my son and my brother, were shot in their heads as they were positioned. If the Judges would allow me, I would like to show you their pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these pictures that were taken at the time, Mrs. Malaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photographs that we received later, I have them with me. My husband, my son, my nephew, my brother, I have the pictures of all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps what we'll do is let Mr. Djordjevic finish his questions and then Mr. Neuner may want to follow that up. He will be asking you some further questions later. So we'll wait for a moment, ma'am. Carry on, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge. In the meantime, as regards the objection of my colleague Mr. Neuner, we've discussed it, and Mr. Neuner is completely right as regards the reference. The Defence was mistaken in its reference. So regarding what the witness said about heading to Meja, what my colleague said, it is completely correct, but there was some permutation of data in the course of our work on this case. We're talking about the statement of the 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2000. This is when it was stated that the police cursed her and insulted her and that then they took their tractors and headed towards Meja. That's at page 3, paragraph 1, first sentence. Of course this is the place where they stopped later. It's practically the same place. And since the witness did not mention, to the best of the Defence's knowledge, that they were ordered to go to Albania but only to Meja, this is why we asked this question. And I have to apologise once again to you and to everyone in the courtroom for this inversion that we made. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. I hope the witness will appreciate that you have apologised that what she actually did say in her original statement was that she was ordered to go to Albania, which is what she has told us here again today. Could we mention, Mr. Djordjevic, that it is a matter of concern that if you're putting to a witness that something materially different was said in a previous statement, there needs to be great care about that; that strictly the proper way to be to show the witness the previous statement, have them look at it and see what they said, and then comment on any difference. Now, we've been allowing you to short-cut that procedure a little by just saying what you understand the witness to have said before, and that can be very unfair to the witness if you haven't accurately identified what was previously said. We will keep this matter under observation, and in the meantime I ask you to be particularly careful when putting to a witness that there's been a change in what they have said from statement to when they gave evidence. Thank you. Now you're moving on with your questioning of the witness, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is because I want to be very careful that I have to say that when it comes to the witness's statement that I've just referred to - and the date is 31st August and 1st September 2000 - which was provided to the investigators Paolo Pastore Stocchi and the interpreter was Valentina Kumnova, on page 2 out of the total of 6, and at the beginning of page 3, second paragraph, there's no reference to Albania. The only reference is made to the village of Meja, nothing else. And that's why the Defence faced the witness with that, calling upon an erroneous statement of the 6th of September, 2001. And this statement is of 31st August and 1st September 2000. And we're going to propose for these statements provided by the witness should be admitted into evidence by the Chamber. I'm talking about the 31st August statement and 1st of September statement 2000, and also the statement given on the 6th of September 2001. And now let me just look at the 65 ter list to be able to give you the numbers of these documents. The first witness's statement, given the 6th of September, 2001, is number from e-court, the English version, D001-3935; and B/C/S is D001-3941; and the Albanian version is D001-3947, for the minutes of the 6th of September. And the second document is marked as D001-3917 in English; B/C/S is D001-3923; and the Albanian version is D001-3929, or 3954, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The second document is D001-3917.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We would have no objection having both statements tendered into evidence, Your Honours, so you can see yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could we indicate both to Mr. Neuner and to Mr. Djordjevic that in accordance with decisions of the Appeals Chamber, the normal procedure in this is not to receive into evidence earlier statements; to simply rely on what is put to the witness in cross-examination from a previous statement as accurately reflecting the relevant part of that statement, and we then have the witness's comment on that. However, in this particular case, as there was a confusion as to what was said earlier, it may be safer for us to receive the two statements. We'll do that on this occasion, but I would like both counsel to be aware that that will not be the usual course followed. We will receive the two statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one, Your Honours, dated the 6th of September, 2001, will be assigned P -- D00025, and the other one dated in August would be assigned D00026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's the 31st of August and the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of September. Both dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I proceed with my cross-examination, I would like to apologise to the Chamber for the confusion that I've created quite inadvertently. In future I'm going to pay attention to avoid any such misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the convoy which was moving towards Albania, am I right in saying, based on your statement, that on the 27th of April you were joined by people from the village of Guska on your way from Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People from Guska village were also in Korenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In regard to what you have told us today and bearing in mind the statement that will be admitted into evidence, on page 2, paragraph 5, the last sentence reads: "There were 17 people together with me, and there was also an entire village population of Guska." Let's clarify one thing: Were there only 17 people with you, or was everybody from Guska already in Korenica?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventeen people from my family, my brothers with their families, staying with me, while people from Guska, the entire village of Guska, was in Korenice, but they were in different houses. In my house we were 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malaj. While the convoy was moving towards Albania from Djakovica to Prizren and onwards to the border crossing, did you hear NATO aircraft flying and was there shelling at the time? I know that a convoy did not come under the NATO shelling, but did you hear that there was shelling around the convoy anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our convoy was not shelled or hurt by NATO on that day. We were escorted by the police and the army but not by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did not hear me. Did you hear NATO aircraft flying over Djakovica and Prizren on that day when you were moving in the convoy? I'm not asking you whether the convoy came under shells. I'm asking you whether you heard anything of the sort as the convoy was moving towards the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malaj. Do you know that on the day when you were moving towards the Albanian border there were extensive military activities and fighting in and around Djakovica between the Serbian security forces and the KLA? Are you aware of that? Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that there was activities involving the KLA and the Serb forces, but I did hear of the activities directed against the civilians from the Serb forces. They exclusively dealt with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned that, could you please tell me whether on that day you were ill-treated in any way? Was anything taken or seized from you? Were you harassed as you were moving towards the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the way to Albania. But it sufficed what they did to me while I was at home. They killed my dearest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will agree with you that that is true. Do you know Merita Dedaj? Does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was she in the convoy with you?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did she also go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Up to Bistrazhin we were together. The convoy was huge and we were not close to each other. I know she was in the convoy, but I don't know where she went to and where she stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, do you know that after a conversation with the priest, members of the Yugoslav Army said to those who were on tractors or on other vehicles to proceed towards Albania, and to those who were on foot, that they should return to their homes, to their villages. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on foot the whole time. I don't know what they told to people on the tractors. I wasn't there. But the priest, we called for him. He did his best to negotiate that we go to Osek Pasa or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the second name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the forces didn't let us go. They said, You either go to Albania or you will be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say that you left your house on a tractor?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That day we couldn't take the tractor, neither the tractor nor the cars. I wanted to tell you before, but you interrupted me. We didn't have any cars or tractors. They wanted the cars for themselves and they didn't -- did not allow us to take the tractors. They even didn't allow us to get any food or drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I asked you because I understood yesterday, you said it clear and loud that you were not allowed to take the car, but you were allowed to take the tractor. However, now you've corrected me, and I appreciated that. When with you return to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your statement provided on the 6th of September, and this time I'm going to double-check to be sure, tell me, please, not only in this statement but in the previous ones provided in the year 2000, you were not consistent about some things. You said that some houses in the village were damaged after you were expelled to Albania and yours was torched. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just out of caution, before the witness answers, could we please have the references. It's some kind of suggestion you're making here to the witness, and we don't have a page number --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course, I'll oblige immediately. Page 5, or rather the last page in all the versions - the English, the B/C/S, and the Albanian - it's the last paragraph, or the second on the page. "I returned to Kosova on the 3rd of July, 1999. Some houses in the village were damaged after our departure and expulsion to Albania. When I returned I found my house had been burned down, and there was nothing there for us," and this is what I mentioned in my question, and this is the record of the statement given on the 31st of August -- I apologise, the 6th of September, 2001, and signed in September 2001. This is what I'm reading on the record, but the record was made on the 6th of September. It says that some houses were damaged and hers had been torched. This is actually the end of my cross-examination of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: You said that some houses had been damaged, and as far as I can understand, there were 70 families in the village, but I did not understand how many houses there were in the village. The fact that there were 70 families does not have to mean that there were as many houses.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole village -- I'm going to speak about my house first. So my house, the whole neighbourhood, the whole village, was burned down. Maybe only ten houses escaped the damage or were not burned, ten houses in all. All the other houses were burned down, starting from my house, including my house, and all the other houses. And when we were leaving, I could see the smoke coming out of them. I told you yesterday, when we were leaving, about 15 houses were burning at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malaj. You actually repeated something that you already said yesterday, and that's why I wish to ask you this: In the statement that I showed you today, why did you say that some houses were damaged when you returned? When you say "some," one might conclude that it was 10 to 20 percent and the rest were okay. And today you're saying that the whole village had been burned down? Can you please explain the difference in the statement that you provided back then and what you are saying now?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole village was burned down. Only ten houses escaped at the time. All of them were burned. Even the houses that were only damaged, they were uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday, you said it just a minute ago, and you have just repeated it. I still haven't got a clear answer to my question. When you were providing your statement, why did you say that some houses were damaged, and now for the third time you're repeating that the whole village had been torched? I see a difference here, and I'm asking for an explanation, if you can provide one. If not, I'm not going to insist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness seems to be saying that the whole village -- excuse me a minute, please, that the whole village was burned except perhaps for some ten houses. I think the whole, less ten, is the way she's putting it, rather than the whole. Perhaps the witness might like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly how I understood it, Your Honour, twice today and once yesterday; however, I face the witness with her own statement in which she stated on the last page, on the fifth page of the record, that some houses were damaged. She never mentioned that the whole village had been torched. And my logical question arising from this is how come she did not mention back then, when she was providing her statement, that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the whole village had been torched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... damaged when it is burned down and the house is uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any more questions for this witness. I see that the witness has had a very hard time being reminded of the tragedy she went through. I am not going to insist on this last answer, although I did not get a clear answer from Mrs. Malaj. I would like to apologise to Mrs. Malaj for any embarrassment that I might have caused her with my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would just ask, because the -- there was some overlap between the translations, that the witness may repeat her last answer. Because I checked the transcript, and I see only five, six words here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat what you said a moment ago, because the translators couldn't catch it, please.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't -- well, you were speaking here about damaged houses. These are houses that were uninhabitable. All of them were damaged and burned. Only ten houses were not. Most of them were uninhabitable, damaged, burned down. Myself, as a person, I went to my home, and I couldn't live in my home. I went to Kosova but not to my home because I couldn't live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you, for the ten houses who were not burned down, how were they damaged?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doors were broken down, windows were broken, furniture had been trashed, walls had been damaged. Everything inside was damaged, and the houses were looted, television sets and other things. But I didn't mention these things in the statement, but these things had happened. We could see that when we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, just relating to the tractor, you mentioned that on the 27th of April you -- 1999, you left also your tractor behind. When you returned, where was your tractor?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't find it there. It had been taken. The cars were burnt --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm just asking for the tractor.

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not there in our courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you manage to recover the tractor since?

utterances.speaker: LIZANE MALAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To this day we haven't been able to recover it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be very pleased to know, I'm sure, that that completes the questioning for you. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give. We appreciate that it is a very big strain for you to have to go over these events, and we will look with care at the evidence that you've been able to give to help us. So we would thank you very much, and the court officer will now assist you and show you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next Prosecution witness is Mr. John Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney will be testifying about the allegations in paragraph 75(C) and paragraph 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have Mr. Sweeney brought into court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you please read the affirmation which is on the card now being passed to you, Mr. Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You could sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you, to your right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: John Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before I start with my questions, since we're both going to be speaking the same language today in court, I just want to ask you to pause between question and answer so the interpreters in the courtroom can do their job properly. Sir, where and where were you born? When and where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I was born in Jersey, the Channel Islands in 1958.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand that you're a journalist by profession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long have you been working as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Oh, crikey. Since 1977 off and on. It was before I went to university I had my first job, The Economist, and full time since 1981, which is whatever that is, 20 years, 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: The BBC. I work for Panorama, which is the main investigations TV programme on British television.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And since when have you been working for the BBC?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Since 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your capacity as a journalist, have you ever covered events in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I started reporting from Belgrade, Vinkovci, Osijek, Dubrovnik, the siege of Dubrovnik, in 1991, in 1992, the war was started in Sarajevo, and I covered the story fully from 1991 through to 1994, and then I went back to Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
