utterances.text: And can you tell us what your work in Kosovo was about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Essentially I -- I had, if you like, two jobs. My first job was that I was a reporter for The Observer newspaper, and I had to write a report pretty much every week of what was going on. At the same time I got a commission from channel 4's Dispatches programme to do a story about a massacre. Essentially what happened was that if you remember the time scale of this, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When -- could you tell us when this happened, when this --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yeah. There was the Serb -- the Serb army attack, led by President Milosevic, took place in the spring of 1999. Albanian refugees in the hundreds of thousands fled to Albania. And as journalists, we couldn't get into Kosovo because the Serb authorities prevented us from doing our job and some people just couldn't get visas. Because of my previous reporting, I was pretty sure I wouldn't get a certain visa or any real meaningful freedom to report. So you were stuck on the other side, on the Albanian side. And it was there that I saw, when I was working for The Observer, I saw a group of exhausted men. We were quite close to the Albanian Kosovo border, on the Albanian side, obviously, and I talked to these men, and they had said they had been -- they had escaped from a massacre of their friends and relatives, in Little Krusha, Mala Krusa, in Albanian, Krusha e Vogel, and that event stuck in my mind. It is always better, in my experience, when you've got a huge thing happening to concentrate on one particular story, rather than getting lost in the mass of it. So I went back to Tirana, and channel 4 Dispatches said, Right now, let's do this story, it sounds good. And then we toured Albania trying to find surviving witnesses to this massacre at Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when it was that you came across this group of refugees who told you about --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: It was -- I believe it's April 1999. It was immediately before their Easter holidays. Sorry, it could well have been March. I believe our programme appeared in May. So those dates, I'm sure there is paperwork where you can -- you can see this. But it's hard for me to remember -- I don't want to say something precisely and then be wrong. But I believe it was March, April when I met these chaps, and then we went looking in April and the programme appeared in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain a bit more of how you went about trying to find witnesses or survivors of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: The story was that there was a man with burnt hands and he had hidden underneath the dead bodies. The whole of Albania was cram-packed, jam-packed with Kosovo refugees, some 800.000, I believe, had fled, some huge numbers of people, and they were staying in schools, in sports halls with relatives all over the place. And there was no rhyme nor reason, no logic, no central pooling of information. So what we had to do was track them down. And I went around saying, Is anyone here from Mala Krusa or Krusha e Vogel? And finally we started to track down witnesses, and we found the man with the burnt hands, and we found the women --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I stop you there just so we can play a clip from your documentary you produced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 0114, and we're going to see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm finding it very difficult to catch what you're saying, Ms. Kravetz. I'm sorry, could you just keep your voice a little a little up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. I think I'm a bit far from the microphone today. We're going to play a short clip. This is 65 ter 0114.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: But there are so many claims of massacre. What's needed is hard evidence. We set out to uncover what really happened in just one small place. We set out to find someone who didn't just hear of the killing but saw it with their own eyes. We set out to name the killers. Albania, Europe's poorest country, has had to cope with an avalanche of humanity, finding anyone from Little Krusha, just a thousand souls in the chaos of half a million of refugees is not going to be easy. "We are looking for people from Krusha e Vogel. We are looking for people from Krusha e Vogel. "To help me I called up an old friend, the writer Agim Neza, who knows his way around."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall when these images that we just saw were filmed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: They would have been filmed in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were you when we saw you there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I think that was some kind of reception centre for refugees. From memory, I think that could well be Tirana. I'm not sure. Because as -- we went looking around the whole of Albania. We were based in Tirana, so it was the obvious place to start. I think we ended up in Elbasan. But there were -- there was an awful lot of refugees, and we did an awful lot of digging before we found people, because it was like looking for a needle in a haystack.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was the situation in other refugee camps you visited similar to the conditions we saw here in this clip?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that was -- essentially things were desperate to begin with because there were so many people and the weather was worse. So when they originally came over the mountain side, the -- eastern Albania, close to the border with the former Yugoslavia, is very poor, very backwards. There's no facilities. So people's lives are desperate. As they got down towards Tirana, things were better. So with those conditions actually are some of the better conditions of some of the refugee camps. As time -- you know, as the weeks went by, things got better, but life was grim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us you were able to find some eye-witnesses to the massacre. Could you tell us what -- what they told you had happened in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I need to be very precise about what we saw and what we filmed. There was a large number of women and children who witnessed the selection, which is men -- you know, men to one side, men and boys to one side; women and the younger children and the younger boys to the other. So they, in a sense, did not witness the massacre itself. What they saw was the selection, and they said, they identified some of their Serb neighbours. Even though they had balaclavas on, they could tell who they were because they lived with them for so many years. Also, we were looking for a group of -- a tiny group of men, who I understand were six, who had actually been in the hay barn, the Batusha hay barn, had been machine-gunned but had managed to survive by hiding -- by falling first and avoiding the bullets and being protected by the dead on top of them. And what happened with the hay barn is that after the machine-gunning, I was told, that the barn was set on fire, and one of these man had burned hands. I believe his name is Mehmet Krasniqi, or Batusha. We found him, and he was the first guy. And then we found two or three other of the survivors, and we put those in our film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to play a second clip from this same exhibit, if we could proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: At last we were about to meet a witness of the ethnic cleansing at Mala Krusa. This is all that is left of the Batusha family; grandmother Batusha, the wives of her missing sons, and their youngest children."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you comment on the images we just saw? Who were these women and children who were on this video?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: The old lady is Granny Batusha, and she lost a number of her sons. One of them was working on a building site in Germany, and he survived. But many of her men in the family, either husbands and the older sons of the women in the picture, they'd all been killed in the massacre. I believe I'm right in thinking that she lost eight men or boys. So you see the women, and there are no men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to locate these members of the Batusha family?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: We kept on asking, and eventually we found somebody who knew where they were, and I think they were staying with relatives in Elbasan. So having found the house, we went to the house, and we knew we were -- we found a family who had been directly affected by the massacre. So essentially the -- the story which I'd started with, these were people who knew what had happened because they had witnessed -- the women and children, they hadn't seen the massacre. They'd seen the selection and then heard the machine-gun fire, so they were good witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did these women tell you anything about who was responsible for the killing of the men in the Batusha family?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. They identified them. Remember, this is a village half Serb, half Albanian, which had been very peaceful, and so that the problems which had visited both communities before in 1998 hadn't happened in that part of Kosovo and in particular in that village. So they were still friends and -- they thought they were friends, and they knew the villagers very, very well. They lived with them all their lives. So even if you stick a balaclava on, you can still tell somebody from the way they walk and so forth. In particular, they singled out a number of people, one of whom was Dimitri. He's an old silver-haired man. And Sava Nikolic, Sveta Tasic, those were two other names that I recall. We didn't have faces; we didn't have photographs of them. It was difficult to work out, and obviously in television you want to find faces. You want to show faces of these people. So what I was determined to do when NATO was actually going into Kosovo was to go to Mala Krusa and find out more and find out for myself, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you were filming this documentary that we just saw, were you able to enter Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: No, it was impossible. It was impossible to do it safely. Some people had -- I know there were some western journalists who were in Belgrade. My problem is that my track record as being a previous critic of the Milosevic regime and that of my newspaper would have made it difficult for me to enter Serbia, and it was even more difficult to get into Kosovo. For me it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When was this broadcast aired or this documentary aired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I believe it was aired in May. I'm sorry to be fuzzy. I can't remember the precise date, but I think it was roundabout May the 20th. The Milosevic indictment was announced a couple of days after our programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the name of this documentary we just saw clips of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm -- the second one is called "Prime suspects." I think this one is called "Witness to Murder." I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. How did you proceed to interview the different persons that you met in Albania when you were preparing this first documentary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: We had a translator, obviously. I don't speak Albanian. And we would sit down and talk to people. The women, we interviewed all at the same time. As time progressed, it struck me that as well as doing a piece of journalism here, there was something more, actually that we were -- in a place that we were ahead of the war crimes investigation, because I knew there was going to be a war crimes investigation, and it struck me that it was important, as much as we could, to interview key witnesses separately and away from other people, as much as we could, because we wanted to get their evidence on its own and to be, if you like, as correct and forensic and evidential as possible. So when we did track down the people who had actually been in the hay barn and survived, the plan was to try and interview them on their own or in very small numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did the accounts of the different persons you interviewed in relation to this incident corroborate each other, or were there disparities between the different accounts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: There's always a small number of little conflicts, but essentially the story as told was corroborated by each other. And the story was, and I think the numbers -- my numbers are right, but I believe there was 109 men and boys were selected, taken to the hay barn. Then, they told me, the survivors told me, the machine-gunner came, and he was late and he -- all of the men were facing with their backs to the machine-gun, with their hands over their heads like that. They actually showed that. The machine-gun blasted away. The survivors fell down very quickly and then other men fell on their -- fell on top of them. And many of the men were not immediately dead, and they could hear the groans. Then the barn was set on fire and most of the Serb killers had run away. And then the last few survivors ran out of the barn and ran away and they managed to escape. So that is the kind of fundamental story which everybody who -- all of the survivors told, and it was corroborated in some way by the women and children who had seen the selection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did these different persons that you interviewed give you any indication as to when this massacre had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. Again the dates -- I haven't got my original notebooks with me. The precise date is on the -- the precise date is I think in the film, but I don't want to -- I can't remember it off the top of my head right now, and I'm frightened of saying something which might be wrong. So I'll -- can I get back to you? Can I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this documentary, this exhibit, at this time. It's P -- it's 00114. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on to a different topic, so I wonder if we could take the break early, just because I want to show some other clips, and they will be interrupted if we begin with them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the second break now and resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was having some problems with my headphones. That's why I was speaking so softly before, but now that's been solved, thanks to my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, before the break you were telling us that while you were investigating this first documentary, you were determined to go to Kosovo and find out for yourself what had happened at Mala Krusa. Did you eventually make it in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. With the -- when the British Army went into Kosovo, I went with them. I rode on the front of a tank. We arrived in Pristina, and I did my stuff for The Observer. And then after a few days in Pristina, I met up with a cameraman James Miller, and we went down -- I believe we went to Prizren first, established a base, and then went the next day to Mala Krusa. Remember what's happened here is that we've actually -- we arrived in Mala Krusa before everybody else did, because most of the Albanians were still -- the Kosovars were still back in Albania because they hadn't been given the all-clear to come back to their homes. So we arrived, and we were ahead of the majority of the survivors, and we saw a scene of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall approximately when it was that you entered Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm thinking the 14th of June. Is that -- that was the very first day when NATO went in. I went in with NATO, so I believe that's the 14th of June. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is -- well --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And so anyway, it's mid-June, but it's the first day, and we went in to Kosovo. Now, lots of Kosovo was intact, i.e., you drive past and you wouldn't be able to see that there had been some kind of war taking place, and certainly that's true of the hinterland towards Pristina. When you went toward Prizren, Mala Krusa, places like that, there was a complete difference, from the Albanian homes - and we heard from people that they were Albanian homes - but you could see they'd lost their roofs, they'd been burnt down, they'd been wrecked and destroyed. And the Serb homes were at that point intact and the Serbs who had been living in them were -- if they were in a large village of community where they felt safe, they stayed. But most of the rest had fled. So when we arrived in Mala Krusa, the village was empty. All the Albanian homes were gutted, without roofs, burnt, and the Serb homes were empty but intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you had prepared a second documentary which was called "Prime Suspects."

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What does this documentary deal with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: This documentary dealt with the -- the story -- it took the story further on. Essentially we -- for the first time we were able to see for ourselves what had happened in Mala Krusa. We were able to see the site of the Batusha hay barn where the machine-gunning had taking place. We were able to see the homes and get the geography, and I was able to go into the Serb homes -- remember, as a journalist, I was looking for photographs. I wanted to put a face to these names. And for that reason I was looking for things like passports, and what I found was army passbooks. But essentially we did a much more detailed film, and we were able to put faces and names to the people who did the killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to play a second -- a third clip, and this is a clip from Exhibit 6 -- 00115, if we could view that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: It's mid-June. The war is over. Hours after NATO rolls into Kosovo, I'm close on their heels. The Serb forces are retreating, but liberation comes too late for 10.000 murdered Albanians. "Krusha e Vogel? Krusha e Vogel? "Our murder inquiry starts at the scene of the crime. This is Little Krusha, a ruin of a village in a ruin of a country. You can't get to the bottom of 10.000 murders. You can try with a hundred. Little Krusha is empty, abandoned, yet full of ghosts. This is the aftermath of ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, are these images we saw just now part of the second documentary that you filmed regarding the massacre in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we saw a series of destroyed houses on the screen. How many of the houses in Mala Krusa looked like the ones we just saw there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: It's hard to -- I don't want to put a precise number on it, but I would say dozens, so in the region of something like at least 20 or 30 houses of the sort were gutted, were wrecks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us that you saw destruction of Albanian homes but that Serb homes had been left intact. How were you able to tell which ones were the Serb homes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, because of the nature of what happened, the Albanians had run away to Albania, the majority of them and left their homes empty, and then they'd been burnt, as I understand it. So they weren't around to defend their homes so that the -- one became very used at that precise time in thinking that if it -- if a house had no roof, it had been -- it was Albanian, and if a house was intact, it was Serb. Now, what happened later was that as it -- as the Albanians came home into Mala Krusa, they realised that the Serbs weren't going to come back because of the massacre, and then they decided to burn the Serb homes, and we also put that in our film. But when I first arrived, all the Albanian homes, it seemed to us, were wrecked and not the Serbs. There had been -- some of them had been kind of looted. I went into -- I went to some of the Serb houses and people had -- the Albanians had come in and sort of rummaged around, possibly looking for money. They'd certainly sort of put clothes and stuff, so that they looked messy, but essentially the buildings were intact, hadn't been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you gave us a date earlier of mid -- sometime in mid-June.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That would be the time when -- was that the time when these images we saw were filmed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're talking about -- if NATO went in on the 14th of June, if I'm right - it's either the 12th or the 14th, I can't be quite sure - then the week -- basically as quickly as possible, so within a -- I think on the Sunday, that would be the 15th, I went to Prizren and, therefore, we started filming the 16th. Remember, this is a film where we -- when you make a film you shoot images all the time and then you edit them, so not every image will have been taken in a kind of linear sequence. Having said that, when we interviewed people, we were pretty -- we make a lot of effort to be correct about that. So we wouldn't jump-cut an interview or get it completely, the timing, wrong. The film is essentially linear in that this happened and then this happened and then this happened. So first arrival, mid-June. Albanian homes in Mala Krusa destroyed by fire, and the Serb houses were empty. The Serbs had left, but their buildings were intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you were able to find the barn where you had heard this massacre had taken place. How were you able to find the Batusha barn?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: It fooled us as first. We didn't see it. There was no barn. There were two holes in the ground. There was a field and two holes in the ground. Later, a few days later, it rained heavily and the water appeared and that's where I believe there's some still photographs of it. But essentially we didn't know what we were looking at. We were looking for a hay barn because the women and children had described the hay barn, but we didn't know that it had been dynamited. But we kind of deduced that when somebody said, No, no, no, it's here, it's here, it's here. And then looking at the image of the hay barn, it seems to me that at some point the Serb soldiers dynamited the hay barn, and you got a kind of blast effect. there's a building against which it was leaning and there are two holes in the walls of that building, and that's -- I've been to lots of war zones, so this is an educated guess, but they put some dynamite in, and the force of the explosion blew those holes in the brick-work of the adjoining building. There was -- if you see, there was a boot. Somebody left a boot. I believe there was a couple of bones. Now, they could be animal bones or human bones, I don't know, but it looked suspicious. And that was it. There was no -- there were no dead bodies; they'd all gone. So it was a, you know -- we -- I don't know what I was expecting, but what we found was, it seems to -- it seemed to us at the time, a deliberate attempt to destroy the evidence of mass killing. By the way, in the clip I'd spoke of 10.000 deaths. Now, the film, I believe, went out in September. Again, I'm guessing; I can't be sure of that. And at the time 10.000 deaths was the best journalistic estimate, and obviously the war crimes tribunal, other people hadn't done their work. I understand the number is around 5.000, between 3.000 and 5.000. That's a more correct number. So obviously the 10.000 number that I cited in the film then, may well be wrong. Obviously that was the -- it was the best journalistic estimate we could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you said the film went out in September, you're referring to the second --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: The second film. It went -- obviously, we -- it could have even been October. I'm not sure. It's ten years ago, so I can't remember precisely. But essentially what happened was from mid-June, I stayed there for a month. And my friend and colleague, the cameraman, Jonas Miller, he, I believe, stayed on longer or came back for a second visit while I was on holiday with my kids. So there is -- there are some scenes which are at the end of the film where I wasn't physically present, but he shot them. In particular, this is the burning of the Serb houses by the Albanians. It's in the film. I wasn't physically there, but you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this burning of Serb houses by the Albanians happened approximately when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm talking roughly, but it's something like four weeks after June the 14th, so sometime in July, late July when I was -- when I was on holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to play a further clip from this same documentary, if we could proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: The trail of evidence begins with the hay barn. But where is it? The village is full of gutted hay barns. One of the first refugees to return is someone who had actually survived the machine-gunning. Everything he owned is ashes, and that is not the worst of it. Xhemajl Shehu [phoen] lost 40 members of his family. He knows exactly where the hay barn is. The last time Xhemajl had taken this path he had been forced at gunpoint along with 111 men of his village. The hay barn isn't here anymore. Instead, just a crater. No bullets, no blood, no bodies. The Serbs had blown it up. "I still find it hard to believe that I'm alive. I wished they'd killed me rather than my sons. Here I lost two of my sons, three brothers, and five nephews. Altogether 40 of my family were killed. Now I have to look after what's left of my family. "This man, Rasim Batusha is the owner of a hay barn. He is alive because he was away working on a building site in Germany. Now everything is gone. Twenty-two of Rasim's relatives were murdered here, among them his three brothers and his eldest son."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, in those images we saw one of the survivors of the massacre. How were you able to locate this person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Essentially we would spend the whole day, every day, in Mala Krusa for about a month, and so we would meet -- we'd meet people, and I'm sure we met Mr. Shehu in the village. Obviously, we were -- we wanted to hear his story and we filmed him. We filmed an interview with him, and then we would sort of see him around. But we were -- we wanted -- obviously, as a journalist, a simple focal point, we wanted to talk to survivors of the massacre. Mr. Shehu was a good witness. He's not a particularly vivid man. I don't mean that to be a criticism of him. It's just that he's perhaps -- well, he'd been through a terrible thing. So we -- having interviewed him, we were still on the lookout for more witnesses who could describe the sequence of events leading up to the massacre and what happened afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We just saw images of the crater on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned that some days later it had rained.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So was the crater later filled with water?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. There were two holes -- essentially there were two holes in the ground, maybe two sticks of dynamite, I don't know, but -- and they later filled -- it rained heavily one day, and it filled with water. So the pictures you've shown me earlier are of -- there is water in the holes. So when we first arrived there was no water, so those photographs were taken after we'd been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the next step in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, we continued to -- what we wanted to do was put names to faces, so we'd heard in Albania about Dimitri -- the reason we'd heard about Dimitri Nikolic was that Granny Batusha recognised him, and she actually -- because after the selection, he had appeared, again I believe wearing a balaclava, but obvious to someone who had known him all his life. And she said, Dimitri, as if -- well, she was expressing her outrage and her shock and disgust that, this man who'd been a neighbour all his life, had taken part in the killing of her family. And so we were looking for him and physical images of him so we could put them on the tele, obviously, and in the newspaper. And Sveta Tasic, Sava Nikolic, and so we had two or three names, and as time wore on, we built a bigger and bigger picture. We also came across two pieces of evidence which were a -- what appeared to us to be a rota, like a guard rota. I'm mentioning that they had the Serb men put themselves into some kind of -- in English we'd call it a home guard arrangement, and we found one piece of paper and were given a notebook by an Albanian lady who knew we were looking for this stuff, which was -- set out this rota. So there were two separate pieces of information. I picked up the first one -- I picked up the piece of paper myself, and we got the notebook from one of the Albanian women who had been away, who had come back, who had been away from Albania and come back, and she found it. And also, we went into -- I went into the empty Serb houses before they were torched by the Albanians later and looked for -- I was looking for photographs and films and home movies or whatever, so we could see these people, and that's how I came across the army passbook.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see another clip from this same documentary, if we could play that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: I've got to be careful. The Serbs have left booby-traps all along the place. Mines are still claiming lives here. Our first break, photographs from the Nikolic family album. There appear to be as many Nikolics in Little Krusha as there are Sweeneys in Donegal. "Our second break, a handful of Serb home videos. With a bit of luck, our suspects might have starring roles. "Our third break, Nikolic Sava. Sava Nikolic. The Serbs were outnumbered 10:1 in Kosovo. They were the ones with the fire power. Nearly every Serb, man, and boy in the village was armed and mobilised in the local militia. The Serb militia were careless. They left this behind. It looks like a scruffy exercise book, but it's material evidence. In it are a series of names of soldiers who were on guard in Little Krusha after the massacre. Amongst the names are two that are becoming all too familiar: Sveta Tasic and Sava Nikolic. "And there's another find. The duty rota, another item of material evidence. It's astonishing they've left this behind. This list identifies 24 names, making up three militia platoons in Little Krusha. Some we know have formed. The document places all 24 men on militia duty in the village. All of these men know something about the clean-up operation. Some of them know something about the murders. All are suspects now."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, I'm losing my voice. In the clip we saw you entering a house. Whose house was that that we saw you entering?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I believe the first house -- basically that's a compilation of shots. I believe the first house is Dimitri Nikolic's house, and the second one is Sava Nikolic's house. It's a long time ago so I'm -- that is my memory. It may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who informed you that these were the houses of these two men?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: The Albanian people like Mr. Shehu who said that, That's where Dimitri lives and that's where Sava Nikolic lives. It was a kind of -- it wasn't a very difficult exercise because one knew what the Serb houses were, partly because some of them had Cyrillic, Serbia united will never be defeated, the four Ss and some of them -- and all of them were intact, they hadn't been burned down. So essentially I think what I did was I went to all of the houses in the centre of the village which were intact. There was a risk to this, and in some ways I was bloody lucky, there was in the village -- we did find that there was a stream, and we went and looked at it. And there was a trip wire for a booby-trap connected to a grenade, which had I tripped it would have blown off, and I might not be here. So we didn't know for a fact whether they had booby-trapped their own homes. Our hunch was that they left in such a hurry once NATO had come in, that they left very, very quickly, and that's what happened. But it was a slightly nervous operation going into these houses because you didn't know whether we'd come across a booby-trap.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we saw you holding a notebook in one of those images. Is that the notebook you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was provided by a local Albanian woman?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we also saw you with a separate sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was something you discovered yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. It was in a house -- it was in a Serb house lying around. I didn't -- I can remember picking it up. I can't remember which house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 02328 up on the screen. Oh, we can't? Is there a problem? I can show it to the witness if there's a technical problem. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue is whether you're going to exhibit the film clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I am, but I'm going to continue -- we're going to view it later, but I can show the two exhibits later, to the witness. It's no problem. We can continue with the video-clip for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, what did you do with the photographs that you found in this house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: We took them back to London, and we had -- we actually had an embarrassment of riches because we had loads of home videos of the Serbs of Mala Krusa, plus the passports, plus the photos or whatever, so we -- we selected -- having heard from the Albanians who their -- who were the people they knew, they recognised, the women and the -- the surviving women and children recognised from the selection, and so we put those in the programme, and then we gave all of the material to the -- to you, to the war crimes tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to the surviving women and children recognising the persons from the selection.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When did this happen, that you showed these photographs to the surviving women and children?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: We -- we did it several times, but again it was -- it was all in this matter of time period. Essentially what happened, and you can see from the film, there is a moment when the Batusha family come back from -- from Albania, and they arrive -- and remember, this is the first time. they never saw the massacre. They only saw the selection and then heard the machine-gun. So they fear their men are dead and that their men and sons and boys are dead, but they don't know it as a fact. So it was a horrendous scene to witness, and you can see it in the film, the women are screaming. But this is the first time that they realise that their men are dead. They also, when they left, their homes were still upright. Some were being burnt, but they hadn't seen the level of destruction. So they come home and they realise their homes are burnt to cinders, and their men are still missing, and the hay barn is a hole in the ground. So there's this sort of ghastly timing when all of the -- ghastly time when the women of the Batusha family realise what's happened. After that we went on the -- sorry, various things are happening all at the same time. We went on our photograph -- I went to get hold of the photographs and the passbooks and all of that stuff when the village was still empty, before they'd come back. Once they'd settled down and recovered their equilibriums, we went to not just one but a number of the Albanians and said, Who's that? Who's that? And who's that? And various of the Albanians recognised their neighbours, and said, Right, that's Dimitri Nikolic. That's Nikolic. That's Sveta Tasic. So again we were conscious of the war crimes tribunal, and at the back of my mind, I wanted more than one, if you like, one source of information. The more sources of information we could have, the better, the stronger the identification. So we checked it out with a number of people. In Albanian society, men -- the women are used to not -- it's the men who take the kind of public roles or whatever, so we ended up showing the photographs, I think, to Mr. Shehu and one of the other survivors as well. That's the clip that we use in the film, but we did more of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did these different people tell you about the photographs? Were they actually able to identify --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- they'd known these people all their lives. They lived with them. They helped start their cars in the cold, et cetera, et cetera, so they knew them very, very well. And they were immediately able to identify them very, very confidently as the people that they had seen take part in the selection -- these are the women now, take part in the selection which led to the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall who were the persons that they identified as being responsible for --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: There were three --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, but the question is not done yet before the witness is answering. It's making it very, very complicated to write this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The process, I'm afraid, is that there is a consequential translation into a number of languages, and if we don't get recorded on here the full question before you commence the answer, we lose either part of the first question or part of your answer. So if it's possible, both Ms. Kravetz and for you as well, Mr. Sweeney, to try and watch the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been switched off, in my defence. Which button is it? It's that one there. Sorry. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not directly your fault, Mr. Sweeney. The problem's identified. We will now try and pace the question, pause, the answer, so that we don't get ahead of those trying to record and translate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you can just complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you could just complete the answer you were given. I was asking whether the persons you had shown -- who the persons you had shown the photograph to had identified as being responsible for this massacre.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: The people they identified -- in a sense, the film is -- the film is a better memory than mine, but the three names that stick out: Dimitri Nikolic, because he was the head of the -- of the Nikolic clan. He was the old man. Sava Nikolic and Sveta Tasic. And they may not have led the massacre. They were just the best known people the villagers, the women in particular, recognised in -- taking part in the selection. By the way, there's something that happened just in terms of understanding. When this -- the massacre was a consequence or followed the NATO air-strike, the NATO air campaign, which started in the spring. Then the Serbs came, and they arrived, and the villagers -- the Albanian villagers told me that they came from buses. So the men, the Serb -- Serb soldiers came in buses, some of them with Nis plates, so they knew the buses were Nis. This is the Albanians. All of the Albanians ran up into the hills and -- behind the village and stayed there overnight and were kind of persuaded to come back to the village the next day. Everything would be okay. They came back. Then later that day, as I understand it, was the selection and the machine-gunning. So there had been quite a time-frame for the Albanians to recognise their Serb neighbours, and what -- those three men, they placed them there. Now, I don't know who was in charge of the massacre, and I doubt whether Serb farmers who are part-time soldiers would be in charge of it. It's just that the Albanians said, Right, I know him and him and him. So that's the -- that's the strength of the identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could play a further clip from the documentary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: I'd taken a pile of photographs from the Serb houses. I began with a list of four suspects. Now I've got 24. But are any of these mugshots of the men I'm looking for? The next step is to get Mehmet and Xhemajl together to identify the line-up. "Dimitri Nikolic, Momcilo Nikolic, Zvesdan Nikolic, Sveta Tasic, Sava Nikolic. "He was the first to shoot at us. As our families were heading for the mountains, Sava shot at us from his house. "Now we can put faces to names. Sava Nikolic. His comrade in arms, Sveta Tasic. Their friend and neighbour Momcilo Nikolic, and his uncle Dimitri Nikolic. Now we know what the men on our wanted list look like, we can start to track them down. But what exactly is the evidence against them?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we had seen you earlier with a notebook and a piece of paper you had found with what looked like a roster. Were the names of these four individuals that appeared here on our screen on those documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I believe so. Without having the documents in front of me, I can't check that authoritatively. I've hit the right button. So I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in Kosovo after filming these images?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, we were essentially there for -- I was there for a month and my -- which actually, in terms of television time, is a long time. Normally you can make a film, with a budget you've only got so much, and I was here to do a film for, say, two weeks or whatever. But what happened was that we -- so after a month, I left. And I believe that James stayed on or James came out while I was on holiday to film the funerals of the dead men. There had been a change. The UCK, the KLA, had not been around when we first arrived in Kosovo. At the funeral, the KLA presence was very strong. There was an armed guard. And I remember James complaining to me about these so-and-sos from the KLA, because they were getting in all his shots, and they were giving a sense of -- of this being a kind of military event, and also that they were very much in charge. That had not been the case when we first arrived. Then what happened is that we had an undercover Serb reporter working with us who identified where the Nikolics were in Serbia, and she tracked them down and tried to film them. We were hoping to catch Dimitri Nikolic on film, and we -- well, I don't think we got him. We were pretty clear that it was there, but at that time in 1999 it was a very, very difficult -- ask for this undercover reporter to effectively risk her life or potentially risk her life in actually naming these people that were suspicious. But that was the end part of the programme. I, myself, didn't return to Kosovo. Having spent a month there, we had, in fact, too much information about this appalling event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to identify where the Nikolics were? Who provided that information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm not entirely -- well, I don't know the process exactly, but essentially we had -- there was -- that's a question better for our Serb undercover reporter who were the -- there was -- you could find out, I think, once you were in Serbia, once you were Belgrade, you could find out where families were, or roughly where communities had gone to. So it wasn't an impossible job for her because she was Serb and based in Belgrade. So she managed to do that. How exactly she did that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when it was that she tried to track these persons down and --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, it's obviously -- you see, I can't -- from this distance, from ten years on, it's difficult for me to remember precisely. But essentially it's after we finished in Kosovo, we brought the material back to London. Then we sent it on to her. So she -- that would have happened in late July, August, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you had told us earlier that in your view the site where the Batusha barn had been had been blown up. Are you aware of whether there were any attempts made to try to recover the remains of those that had been killed there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: No. I mean -- well, there may well have been -- the problem is this is a -- all one can do is deduce from the evidence on the ground, so what we're looking at is two holes on the ground, but I was looking for bodies. We thought that there were -- we looked all around, and then obviously the river Drina is close by. It's, what, about 2 kilometres from the village itself. So one thing you could do is you could -- if you burned the bodies in the hay barn, set fire to it, you then -- with a tractor, you can dump them in a river. It's a big strong river, lots of snow melt, so it was one place we looked. And we did find the lorry, and I swam in the river, and I thought I saw blood on the side of a lorry. I may have been mistaken. What we didn't find was dead bodies. We looked, but we didn't find any human remains. Hold on a second. We found a few human remains. By this time the war crimes tribunal had arrived, forensic people working for the Tribunal, and I think they found -- they may have found evidence. We never found a big gravesite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that forensic people who were working for the Tribunal arrived. Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: It was around about -- it was towards the end of our stay there, bearing in mind -- so we'd been there from mid-June, and I think I -- for The Observer, I'd had to leave Mala Krusa a couple of times, but I came back to continue filming and looking for evidence. And I believe that they would have arrived in July, early July. That's my guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was your film crew still filming there at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So we filmed -- we filmed them. Their first base was in -- remember, there was a -- there was also a smaller massacre of around, I believe, 20 people, or 12, I can't remember in this distance, in Greater Krusha, which was further up the road, and I believe they went there first, and then they came to Mala Krusa. There was a parallel BBC team filming in Greater Krusha, and I believe that the BBC filmed the war crimes people, and we didn't. I think that's my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we play a final clip from this same documentary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: "THE PRESENTER: Two months after the end of the war, forensic experts from Scotland Yard arrive in Little Krusa. They're working for the war crimes tribunal in The Hague, but they've been busy. There are 10.000 murders to solve in Kosovo. Their task is to find out who was killed and how. There's precious little for them to do at the hay barn, so they're probing what's left of this second murder site in the village. There's not much to go on. A button, a belt, a smear of blood, a backbone."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, you referred earlier to a smaller massacre site being filmed. Do these images correspond to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: No. Sorry, I've just put the LiveNote up. There are three separate events. In Greater Krusha, I have forgotten what it is in Serbian, not Krusa Mala but something else. In Greater Krusha there was a small massacre -- there a massacre, I believe, involving around 20 dead. In Mala Krusa there was the hay barn, in which 103 people were killed and six survived, as I understand it. And then down the road, also in Mala Krusa, but on the other -- sorry, on the other side of the road but still in Mala Krusa, I believe seven people were killed in that house we've just seen. So that's -- the smaller massacre I was just referring to a second ago was in relation to Greater Krusha, not this scene. I believe about seven people were killed there. But yes, I've forgotten, we filmed the war crimes forensic people at that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm being reminded that we need to pause between question and answer. The reporter is having problems recording what is being said because you're starting your answers too quickly and not allowing her to finish typing my questions. So I would just ask you to keep an eye on the screen, and when the cursor stops, you can start with your answer, just to allow her to do her job properly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's okay. So, sir, do you know whether any remains were found at the site of the barn itself by the forensic team that was there conducting its exhumations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Sir, I would --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit at this stage. This is Exhibit 65 ter number 00115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 02328 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have the document before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I believe it's one of the documents that I -- that I picked up. I'm not sure whether it's from the notebook or whether it's the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm not sure whether it's the notebook or the piece of paper. In fact, you probably know better than I do. But that is the -- there are the names, obviously, in the -- you can clearly recognise in the middle, you've got Tasic Sveta, Nikolic Sava, Nikolic Ranko, and they seem to be on the night shift. The date is between the 16th and 17th of April, 1999. My understanding is -- I can't quite remember, but I believe the massacre took place in late March, so this is after the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00299, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now -- could we now please have 65 ter 02327 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, again, it's my guess, you've got three groups here. These are -- if this is some kind of home guard militia, they're -- they're in what looks to be like three guard duties. So one takes a day shift, one takes a night shift. This whole time the Serbs are under the NATO air-strike campaign, and they're afraid that at some point NATO and the KLA will enter Kosovo, as, indeed, they did. And therefore this is the local organisation -- I'm guessing this. I don't know this for a fact. But this is the local organisation of the Mala Krusa Serbian militia, and obviously the names -- you've got the Nikolic family and the Stankovics and the Petkovics. These are all names that the villagers recognised. Again, group II -- to be precise, I don't know who commanded the massacre. It's just that this is what the Albanians told me these are the people they recognised: Sava Nikolic -- again, when Mr. Shehu, Xhemajl Shehu, he is the old man who lost 40 members of his family, he said it was Sava Nikolic who shot at them as they were going up the hill, and that happened on the first day. So remember, there were two days. There's the NATO strike. Then the Albanian villagers leave the village for the hills. They're going away from the river, away from Albania, into Kosovo. They're heading roughly, as I understand it, east into the hills. And at that point according to Mr. Shehu, Sava Nikolic shot at them. That's why his name -- they identify him from his house. The others, Dimitri Nikolic, Granny Batusha saw. So to an extent I was being led by the Albanians into concentrating on these people simply because they recognised them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, is this document and the other document we just looked at the ones we saw earlier in your clip, the clip from the documentary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So would this have been documents that you found or persons found and gave to you during your investigation --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: I think my memory is correct in saying that I found the piece of paper and somebody else handed me the notebook, or the other way around. I can't remember. But I'm pretty sure I found the piece of paper, and an Albanian lady found the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where did you find this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY
utterances.text: In the Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 0232 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00300, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Looking at the time, I think it would be not useful to commence cross-examination, Mr. Djordjevic. So what we will do is adjourn now. We have only five minutes to go. We will adjourn now to resume tomorrow and hopefully to complete the evidence of Mr. Sweeney in the course of that tomorrow. Could I remind counsel that we are sitting tomorrow afternoon. Due to changes with some other trials, we have now been moved to the afternoon, so we will resume at 2.15. Mr. Sweeney, if you would be able to return then to, I hope, complete your evidence, we'd be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of February, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
